C4_positive_control_sharing.expected: Shared patterns (e.g., GET /posts/{id}) collapse to 1 parameterized mechanism
C4_positive_control_sharing.observed: blog-read-post tasks share 1 pattern (GET /posts/${id_0}), 5 tasks sharing

C5_null_control_no_sharing.expected: Unique patterns (no sharing) show no deduplication benefit
C5_null_control_no_sharing.observed: 3 unique search patterns, each used by 1 task only

observations: Mechanism count reduction: 25 parameterized vs 32 literal = 21.88% reduction. The reduction is driven by 3 patterns that are shared across multiple tasks: GET /posts/{id} (5 tasks), GET /products/{id} (3 tasks), GET /orgs/{orgId}/projects/{projId} (2 tasks).
Token cost reduction: 679 parameterized tokens vs 791 literal tokens = 112 tokens saved (14.16%). Deduplication ratio 0.8584 < 1.0, confirming parameterized representation is cheaper overall.

Per-task analysis reveals that deduplication savings are concentrated in tasks that share patterns with other tasks. The 5 blog-read-post tasks each show -15.79% per-task penalty (parameterized costs MORE per task), but the pattern is stored once instead of 5 times.

The critical insight: per-task, parameterized mechanisms often cost MORE tokens (due to ${slot} syntax overhead). But across the corpus, the same pattern is stored once, not N times. The net effect depends on how many tasks share each pattern.

Sharing distribution: 22 patterns used by 1 task (no deduplication benefit), 1 pattern used by 2 tasks, 1 pattern used by 3 tasks, 1 pattern used by 5 tasks. Only 3 patterns (out of 25) provide deduplication benefit.

The admin-view-user URLs (u-aaa, u-bbb, etc.) were NOT parameterized by the heuristic regex, remaining as 5 separate literal mechanisms. A more sophisticated parameter induction system would recognize these as /users/{id} and collapse them, improving the deduplication ratio further.
Search tasks (blog, shop, admin) have unique query parameter patterns and show NO deduplication benefit. Parameterized representation adds tokens for these tasks (-19% to -35% penalty per task).
Kernel regression: 3/3 existing tests pass, no regression.
validity_notes: This is a STATIC ANALYTICAL measurement, not an end-to-end agent workflow measurement. It measures registry storage and token cost, not retrieval efficiency, transmission cost, or amortized agent execution cost.
Task corpus is synthetic/representative, not derived from actual SPIDER agent execution logs. Real agent workflows may have different sharing patterns.

Parameter induction uses a heuristic regex-based approach, not the actual distill_parameterized() kernel function. Some parameterizable patterns (e.g., /users/u-aaa) were not recognized, understating deduplication potential.
Token counting uses tiktoken cl100k_base encoding of JSON-serialized action_template dicts, consistent with parent experiments.
The deduplication ratio measures storage cost (total tokens for all mechanisms), not per-query retrieval cost. In practice, retrieval would only fetch relevant mechanisms, changing the economics.
No browser, model, or network calls. Purely analytical computation in Python 3.12 with tiktoken 0.14.0.
The 14.16% net savings is a LOWER BOUND because the heuristic parameter induction missed some parameterizable patterns (e.g., admin user URLs).
unresolved: Whether end-to-end amortized cost (including retrieval, verification, and repair) also shows savings when fewer mechanisms need to be stored and retrieved
Whether a production-quality parameter induction system would achieve higher deduplication than the heuristic regex used here
Whether the 21.88% mechanism count reduction is sufficient to justify the engineering cost of maintaining parameterized mechanisms
Whether different task corpus compositions (more or less sharing) would produce different deduplication ratios
Whether the per-task token penalty (-15.79% for shared patterns) is acceptable given the corpus-wide savings (14.16%)
